en: The *Anupamapūrṇabodhisattvasūtra*, Scroll One.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling on Mount Vipula in the city of Rājagṛha.
In the midst [of this assembly], he was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus numbering one hundred thousand;
furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, as well as bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, garuḍas, and so forth.
Furthermore, there were various devaputras of the desire realm and various devaputras of the Pure Abodes of the form realm who surrounded him in front as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Asaṃvidyamāna (Non-existent), who was seated in that gathering.

However, within that assembly there were bodhisattvas who harbored doubts in their hearts, those who regretted having committed evil deeds, those who dwelt in perversion, those with karmic obstructions, and those with dharma obstructions; as well as other sentient beings who, being hindered by such obstacles, were unable to question the Buddha.
However, wishing to purify the karmic obstacles of those sentient beings, he desired to ask the World-Honored One:
"Observe this assembly; there are many bodhisattvas who wish to repent for their past evils, yet their minds are so consumed by distress that they are unable to listen to the Dharma."

Furthermore, he saw bodhisattvas who, with minds free from regret or affliction, were able to listen with single-minded attention. He observed that their mental activities were characterized by much suffering and distress, much anxiety and calamity, and much defilement; they were beset by much birth, old age, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, and by much association with the hated and much separation from the beloved. While they sought to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they were nonetheless bound by such immeasurable fetters.
"How shall one practice the bodhisattva conduct throughout incalculable eons?
Since one is oneself bound, how can one possibly liberate the bonds of sentient beings?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nothingness, having reflected thus, immediately contemplated within himself:
“If the Blessed One would grant me permission to ask a question, it is for the sake of all sentient beings in this assembly, so that they may be freed from evil doubts and regrets.

At that time, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva No-Thingness and the entire host of those bodhisattvas, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva No-Thingness, saying: “O No-Thingness!”
I do not speak to the bodhisattvas of defilement, attachment, bondage, fettering, or transgression and the objects of transgression. Why is this?

It is because I wish to cause them to transcend and remain far removed from all points of attachment, all points of defilement, all points of bondage, all points of obstruction, and all points of transgression; so that by practicing non-conjunction, with all phenomena unmixed and ungraspable, they may realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this way, all dharmas are unbound, all dharmas are unstained, all dharmas are unattached, unfastened, unobstructed, untransgressed, and unattained; therefore, one shall realize all-knowledge (sarvākārajñatā).

"Good son! In the place where the mind of omniscience arises, no sentient beings are found. Within that state, there is no dharma that can be bound, stained, attached to, fettered, obstructed, transgressed, attained, or known; therein you have nothing at all!"

You should ask on behalf of all bodhisattvas, so that these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—being untiring, unstained, unattached, unbound, and unobstructed like space; being free from the notion of space and without hindrance—may swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and thus you should reveal and clarify this for them in all places.

At that time, because the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati had been granted the empowerment requested by the Tathāgata, and because he had planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas through his own power of wisdom, he was able to remain free from doubt regarding the Prajñāpāramitā; thus, he concealed his body so as not to appear, remaining without attachment.

Desiring to gather and transform all bodhisattvas, and further wishing to manifest all merits, and for the sake of those sentient beings who are attached—those who act while covered by grasping and signs, who have distanced themselves from spiritual friends, and who are seized by evil associates—the bodhisattvas, knowing that all phenomena are unattainable, and wishing to bring about non-attachment and awakening, scattered immeasurable varieties of flowers upon the Buddha, whether born of water or land, or even flowers of gold and silver.
With a mind of sincerity and joy, supreme and flawless, he praised the World-Honored One so as to inspire joy in all sentient beings,
and asked in verse:
"Where does the Bodhisattva roam?"
Who are their parents? Where do they dwell?
And who are their kinsmen?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin with these verses:
"Bravely roaming in the sphere of emptiness, With Prajñā as mother and the Buddha as father,
Taking the Buddha-stūpas as their dwelling place, And having all bodhisattvas as their retinue."
"Roaming through the six pāramitās, with the bodhicitta as one's parents,
samādhi as one's dwelling place, and all merits as one's retinue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiñcana, having heard these verses from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, rejoiced and followed them in accordance.
Again, he questioned the World-Honored One in verse:
"You are well able to speak these words; O All-Knowing One, you are unimpeded.
I rejoice in these words, And ask again of the Supreme among Men."
What are the causes and conditions?
By what skillful means and wisdom?
And what dharma is touched and realized?
"How should one be aware of this?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the Bodhisattva Nothingness with these verses:
"The courageous conditions for awakening, Skillful means to gather in sentient beings,"
"Having realized the emptiness of all phenomena, the wise awaken to bodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiñcana, having heard this verse, rejoiced and followed it in accord, praising it with a verse of his own:
And he asked again:
"You are well able to speak these words; all-knowledge is unimpeded.
I rejoice in these words; I ask further, O Supreme among Men."
"Why do you not fall into the evil realms?
Abandoning all places of evil, you shall swiftly reach the auspicious realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“By not committing any evil, one thus abandons the evil realms;
by constantly practicing the Dharma, one thus reaches the auspicious realms.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiṃcana, having heard this verse, rejoiced and praised it.
He asked again: "Well-spoken are these words; all-knowing and unimpeded, I rejoice in these words. I ask once more, O Supreme among Men."
"How can those many transgressions, committed in a state of ignorance,
all be swiftly extinguished, so that they are utterly destroyed without remainder?
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to the Bodhisattva Akimcanya in verse:
“Sentient beings seeking liberation, these aspire to bodhi;
because bodhi cannot be attained, all transgressions are utterly extinguished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Anupalipta (No-Attachment), having heard this verse, followed it with joy.
Again, he asked in verse:
"You have well spoken these words, O Omniscient One, free from all obstruction.
I rejoice in these words, And ask again of the Supreme among Men."
"How is it that all attachments, the wandering through the sufferings of affliction,
are completely exhausted without remainder at the time of attaining bodhi?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"In the state of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, one mistakenly grasps at emptiness;
once true awakening as it really is has been attained, all craving shall be exhausted.
Free from the craving of ego-conceit, grasping and so forth will be like empty space."
"Not abiding within or without, they have no place of attainment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nihilist (Anupalaṃbha) rejoiced in this verse and further praised it.
He asked in verse:
"You are well able to speak these words; All-knowing and unimpeded, I rejoice in these words, And ask again, O Supreme among Men."
What karma should one perform so that those seeds—
how they come to be— result in great wealth that is never exhausted,
and such that one is able to give to all, practicing generosity without stinginess?
"One is able to relinquish entirely one's body, flesh, wealth, head, and so forth.
At that time, having heard this question, the World-Honored One provided an explanation for the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, further speaking in verse:
"Always making offerings to the Triple Gem without weariness,"
Furthermore, those wise ones who sever the world and offer worship do so because they have generated the bodhicitta for the sake of bringing happiness to sentient beings.
Bearing the burden of enlightenment, they explain its enjoyment to others.
The All-Knowing One, for the sake of all sentient beings, has taught this;
therefore, he possesses wealth that is inexhaustible at all times.
Having performed such deeds and having planted such seeds, [the fruit ripens].
In every place where one is born, may there be abundant merit and great wealth.
Whether coarse or fine food, having drunk [the water] according to the pure Dharma;
if one obtains new clothing, one shall put it on first for others and afterwards for oneself.
Therefore, throughout all successive births, one will be preeminent in every respect;
without exerting further effort, one shall obtain inexhaustible wealth.
Thus, in all acts of giving, one should practice relinquishment and abandon stinginess.
"His own flesh and even his head—there is nothing he would not give.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akimcanya, having heard this verse, expressed his sympathetic joy and offered praise.
Again, he asked in verse:
“You have well spoken these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom.
I rejoice in these words and ask again of the Supreme among Men.”
"How does one become free from the affliction of heat in body, speech, and mind?
How does one come to possess a supreme form, stainless and most pure?
At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded upon this by speaking in verse:
"Observing the precepts without omission, always speaking of emptiness without defect,
knowing that all things are empty, and enduring all beatings, reviling, and insults through body,
speech, and mind— for this reason, there is no feverish distress."
They shall attain the most excellent form, beloved by all sentient beings.
Briefly stated, among all well-spoken words and among all explanations of questions,
how do they become firm and diligent?
"Since there is no contradiction in any respect, how could there be various vehicles,
whether they pertain to the mundane or the supramundane?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Not timid in performing deeds, And discerning within mental activities,
Therefore, diligence and wisdom Are ever present within that which arises.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akimcanya again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"Well spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
We rejoice in these words and ask again of the Supreme among Men:
How does one possess wisdom that is certain within the world?"
"How does he possess such power that no sentient being is able to subdue him?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"He constantly inquires about the teachings of all Buddhas and does not slander any dharmas."
Seeking all skillful means, he thus possesses supreme wisdom.
Constantly bestowing the five kinds of flavors, he grants fearlessness to sentient beings;
therefore, he possesses power that no sentient being can subdue.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiṃcana asked in verse:
“Excellent is this speech you have spoken, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
I rejoice in these words and ask again of the Supreme among Men.”
"What is that supreme form, most excellent in the world?
How does one attain a long life, lasting for many hundreds of billions of years?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"If one hears of faults, whether true or false, and does not pass them on to others;
if one constantly praises the Triple Gem so that its fame reaches the ten directions;
if one does not afflict sentient beings and does not rejoice in those who kill—"
"Therefore, one attains a long life, lasting for many hundreds of billions of years.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiṃcana again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"You have well spoken these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom."
Rejoicing in these words, he again questioned the Supreme among Men:
"How does one obtain the Brahma-voice and the song of the kalaviṅka?
If there are those who hear it, having heard it, they shall attain joy."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"When preaching the Dharma, one praises [the teaching] and never utters words of disparagement;
one does not cause division among those in harmony— for this reason, one attains the sublime voice."
Guarding against the four kinds of verbal transgressions, always speaking words that are beneficial,
and being able to disclose one’s own faults— for these reasons, one attains sublime sounds.
The sounds of conchs and drums, and the harmonious blending of various musical instruments—
"Having made offerings to all Buddhas, for this reason one attains the sublime voice.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiñcana asked in verse:
"Well-spoken are these words, O embodiment of the perfection of all wisdom."
Rejoicing in these words, he again questioned the Supreme among Men:
"How is it that his body and belly are so well-proportioned and upright,
and how is it that all his retinue are in harmonious accord?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Poisonous drugs and non-medicines, Neither giving them nor instructing others to do so,
But administering decoctions according to the illness— For this reason, the abdomen is level and upright."
Toward both virtuous friends and enemies, he is equal in his radiance;
having established such a mind toward them all, for this reason his abdomen is level and upright.
As for the realm of all sentient beings, there is no limit to their number.
Loving them as one's own self, for this reason his abdomen is level and upright;
Just as parents always give rise to thoughts of compassion for their only child,
so too toward all sentient beings, he thus attains a level and upright abdomen.
The Bodhisattva and his parents, making offerings without weariness,
therefore their retinue always follows them as if they were their own selves;
so too do the World-Honored One and the elders, as well as those who are venerable and superior.
If one serves them with a mind that is disciplined, supple, and humble,
then those attendants will follow one as if they were oneself.
Being free from discrimination, one possesses a mind of universal equanimity.
By gathering others through the four means of attraction, one is able to gather many sentient beings;
therefore, those followers shall become like oneself.
Teaching and practicing various beneficial virtues toward inconceivable numbers of sentient beings—
Therefore, those retinues follow [the teacher] as if they were themselves;
they harmonize with the bodhicitta toward inconceivable sentient beings.
Therefore, those retinues follow [the teacher] as if they were themselves.
There is nothing they do not relinquish for the sake of all sentient beings;
therefore, their retinues and others follow them as if they were themselves.
Toward all sentient beings alike, they shall act with one common purpose.
For this reason, all sentient beings are always together as kinsmen.
Whatever cherished objects one possesses, one is able to give them to others;
without harboring thoughts of loss or discrimination, for this reason, one has many kinsmen.
At that time, Abhāva again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“Excellent is this speech, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
I rejoice in these words and ask further of the Supreme among Men.”
"How can their mindfulness be pure, so that they may proceed toward the boundless?
How can they delight in the Dharma, yet never depart from the True Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"To those who delight in the Dharma he teaches it; to those who have lost the Dharma he causes them to remember it.
Without afflicting sentient beings, he thus practices with right mindfulness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nihilist again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“Excellent is this speech, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
We rejoice in these words and ask again, O Supreme among Men:
How is it that, having heard the Dharma, one remains forever free from doubt?”
"Once one has attained the five supernormal powers, how can they be prevented from being lost?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"To cause sentient beings to be without delusion within the most supreme Buddha-dharma,"
"Those who hear this without doubt shall attain the superknowledges (abhijñā) without loss.
Then, the Bodhisattva Akimcanya again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"Well-spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!"
Rejoicing in these words, he again questioned the Supreme among Men:
"How is it that all bodhisattvas, though constantly in the presence of the Buddhas,
are unable to subdue greed and hatred in their every form?"
"How do afflictions arise?
Upon what basis are they countered? Furthermore, how can one possess a sense of shame and remorse, so that once [afflictions] have arisen, they may be pacified?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Constantly mindful of all Buddhas, yet there is nothing to be mindful of;
not perceiving sentient beings, they speak of bodhi—
therefore they are called Bodhisattvas, always remaining in the presence of the Buddhas.”
Neither destroying afflictions nor departing from the Buddhas,
it is like a wise person looking up at the sky above;
therein is neither body nor mind, for there is no other place apart from that.
When that wise person gazes upon the upper reaches of space,
at that time they have no other thoughts, whether of body or mind.
Thus guarding bodhi, they [attain it] in the presence of all Buddhas.
The body and mind are unmoving, nor are they distant from the Buddhas.
There is no object for false discrimination, yet the afflictions such as desire are aroused;
there is no object that is not discriminated, and therefore it cannot be destroyed.
"When mindfulness arises before one, there is no obstruction because of the absence of mindfulness;
since that which has been relinquished lacks reality, once awakened, these things are relinquished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akimcanya again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"Well spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
We rejoice in these words and ask again of the Supreme among Men:
By what cause is one born through transformation (*upapāduka*), and how does a Bodhisattva always possess joy?"
"When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, one is born amidst various lotus flowers?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"All meritorious virtues bring happiness within the cycle of birth and death."
Sentient beings are born within this; therein, among all the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, are all the pāramitās.
Within all those teachings—both mundane and supramundane—they cause them to awaken to all phenomena.
The characteristics of all phenomena are without characteristic and without a sustainer;
all phenomena abide in this way, and therein he teaches sentient beings.
It is likewise in emptiness and signlessness, and so it is within non-arising.
In this world there is no place for practice; therein he teaches sentient beings.
Therefore, those who are born through transformation, the bodhisattvas, always possess joy.
When the Buddhas preach the Dharma, they are born within various lotus flowers.
When Bodhisattvas cultivate such merit and do not disparage it, for them there is no difficulty; all joys are inconceivable.
Having cultivated this merit, no one is able to disparage the Bodhisattva.
Possessing skillful wisdom regarding all phenomena, there is nothing he does not know.
Having mastery over all phenomena, he perceives them with certainty and without doubt;
for the sake of sentient beings, he speaks [the Dharma] in order to gather them in.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiṃcana, having heard these verses, rejoiced in these words and praised the World-Honored One, asking with a verse:
"Well-spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom;
I rejoice in these words and ask again, O Supreme among Men."
"For what reason does this woman, upon being seen, transform her body into that of a man—
one so upright and pleasing to behold that all sentient beings love and delight in him?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Whatever thoughts women have, whatever objects women cling to, and whatever sounds of women's songs—do not dwell with them. One should take no pleasure in seeing or hearing them;
one should not touch them, for they are like vessels of poison."
Keeping far away from women as one would from venomous snakes, always regarding them with apprehension;
not touching any women and not encouraging others to take on a female body;
by teaching the transformation of the female body, they see it accomplished as a male body.
"Having practiced in this way and abiding correctly in this practice,
when a woman sees [him], she immediately transforms her body into that of a man.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiñcana, having heard these words, rejoiced and further questioned him in verse:
"Well spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
I rejoice in these words and ask again, O Supreme among Men:
By what cause do sentient beings, upon seeing [you], give rise to the mind of enlightenment?"
"And how does one attain non-retrogression, even unto the seat of enlightenment?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"I do not speak of inferior states; I speak only of supreme enlightenment."
Therefore, when sentient beings see this, they immediately give rise to the bodhicitta.
Regarding even the slightest portion of suffering within perception and mental formations, [he realizes] that in reality it has no locus; thus he teaches it to all sentient beings.
At that time, Abhāva again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“Excellent is this speech, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom;
I rejoice in these words and ask further of the Supreme among Men.”
"For what reason, upon seeing one who is ill, do you give rise to a mind of compassion toward them?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Observing that the body is illusory, one has no attachment within it."
This is the medicine of the world; therefore, one is freed from all afflictions.
Because the sick see this, they are cured in an instant;
by giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward them, one thus eliminates all maladies.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akimcanya again questioned the World-Honored One, speaking in verse:
“Excellent is this speech, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
I rejoice in these words and ask further of the Supreme among Men.”
"For what reason do sentient beings see that all their hunger and thirst are entirely eliminated, and they become full, their bodies satisfied and joyful?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“By constantly bestowing abundant food and drink, and further preaching the supreme Dharma for them,
sentient beings who behold this find their hunger and emptiness naturally extinguished.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nihilist again questioned the World-Honored One, speaking in verse:
"Well spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
I rejoice in these words and ask again, O Supreme among Men:
By what means can one become free from attachment, and abandon such views as annihilationism and eternalism?"
"In that which is neither middle nor extreme, how can there even be any abiding or reliance?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Without攀缘 (clinging to objects) or conceptual discrimination, transcending worldly speech,"
"Knowing that all phenomena are equal, one attains freedom from defiled attachment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiṃcana again addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
"Well-spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom."
Rejoicing in these words, he again questioned the Supreme among Men:
"By what cause is it that one perceives evil conduct as able to bind this world?
How can one abandon all realms of existence and purify the retribution of karmic intentions?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"One should draw near to virtuous friends; If one has resolved upon the Bodhi-mind, Therefore, one should leave behind evil conduct And purify the Buddha-wisdom."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akimcanya again praised with verses, asking the World-Honored One:
“Excellent is this speech you have spoken, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom.
I rejoice in these words and ask further of the Supreme among Men.”
For what reason are perception, mental formations, and wisdom all non-existent?
Within the truly empty dharma, how shall they attain freedom from doubt?
For what reason do they obtain eloquence, capable of discerning all phrases?
Knowing the conduct of sentient beings, how does one preach the Dharma for them?
How can one always abide within the four wheels,
avoid falling into the eight unfavorable conditions, and attain this state of leisure?
"What dhūtas should one adopt? What ascetic practices should one perform, so that one will have no evil remorse and furthermore no afflictions?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Sentient beings are attached to conceptual formations; I teach the meaning of them being like a mirage.
Once one has realized emptiness and selflessness, one shall understand all forms of eloquence.
Having realized the truly supreme meaning, one shall leave behind the eight difficulties.”
When the four wheels are fulfilled, the Bodhisattva possesses skillful wisdom.
Having shaken off all acquisitions of existence, he does not engage in superior asceticism;
knowing that the self is empty, he no longer harbors doubt or regret.
"All phenomena are like space; having known this, one does not cling to the world.
Having awakened to the meaning of the inversions, one shall attain the Bodhi of a Buddha.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiñcana rejoiced in these words and again questioned the World-Honored One, speaking in verse:
"Well spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
We rejoice in these words and ask again of the Supreme among Men:
Having heard this, when one has reached a secluded place, how should they dwell?"
"How does one generate the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), and why is it called the most supreme?
At that time, the World-Honored One further explained this by speaking in verse:
"Having heard thus, one generates [the aspiration]; having generated it, one does not abide [in it]."
Those superior and excellent beings shall practice the supreme enlightenment.
If they practice such conduct, they will have no place to dwell;
they shall swiftly awaken to enlightenment, like a person shooting an arrow upward.
These are the three modes of discourse; if one were to awaken to them as they truly are, as being quiescent by their very nature, one would not "practice" for enlightenment.
Whatever is spoken within the sounds of conditioned phenomena regarding the world, [is likewise such].
Since all sounds do not exist, one should know they are not real.
Within that which is unreal, there is no production, and thus action (*saṃskāra*) cannot be apprehended either.
If one can understand it in this way, that person practices the conduct of awakening (*bodhicaryā*).
"Without practice, one takes up practice; yet it is not shallowly blossomed.
Once there is nothing to be perceived, that practice cannot be found.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Nothingness (Anupalaṃbha) asked in verse:
"Well spoken are these words, O embodiment of all-encompassing wisdom!
We rejoice in these words and ask again of the Supreme among Men:
By what cause does one relinquish all bodies so that no suffering whatsoever remains?"
Maintaining equanimity toward all realms, when should one relinquish the practice of life?
Whether lying on the right side, or sitting with legs crossed in the full lotus posture,
or perhaps standing upright, or joining the palms in reverence—
When teaching the profound Dharma, the Prajñāpāramitā,
and all the teachings of the Buddhas— neither abiding in nor extinguishing all phenomena—
some see the time of attaining Buddhahood, while others praise all dharmas.
Listen with a concentrated mind to all that is taught regarding the dharmas.
One shall cast off this present body and subsequently take on a new body;
passing from household to household, one shall give rise to the bodhicitta.
"Without delusion, one tames mindfulness; in a single thought-moment, one dwells correctly in concentration.
"How should one relinquish life, and how should one again manifest supernormal powers?"
Please explain this question for me, O one who possesses an infinite mass of wisdom.
"In brief, it should be understood that all the virtues therein, as taught in the Vinaya, are immeasurable and inconceivable."
All supreme perfections shall be accomplished by them.
As the Teacher has taught me, according to reality and according to the true nature of things—
should anyone hear of these merits, they shall all offer worship.
Having guarded the ten wholesome paths, one will have no doubt regarding the dharma of emptiness;
possessing the fourfold brahma-conduct, all things will be fully accomplished.
One shall not find [grasping] within the six sense faculties, nor within the entire triple world.
Having attained mastery over all things, one will not give rise to doubt regarding what is heard.
One should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like shadows;
one should understand them thus: those shadows have no conditioned nature.
Unconditioned and shadowless, without speech and without discrimination,
without thought and without verbal expression, without stinginess and without giving;
within the unconditioned and shadowless, there is no speech and no discrimination.
Within that which is without thought and without speech, there is neither upholding nor breaking of precepts;
within that which is unconditioned and shadowless, there is neither speaking nor discrimination.
Within that which is without thought and without speech, there is neither contention nor patience.
Within the unconditioned and shadowless, there is no speech and no discrimination;
within the thoughtless and wordless, there is neither indolence nor diligence.
Within the unconditioned and shadowless, there is no speech and no discrimination.
Within that which is without thought and without speech, there is neither distraction nor meditative concentration;
within that which is unconditioned and shadowless, there is neither discourse nor discrimination.
Within that which is without thought and without speech, there is neither folly nor wisdom.
When there is no shadow, nothing further is seen; because nothing is seen, it is called "shadowless.
