Nor should one give rise to such thoughts; this is the Buddha’s supernormal power.
All buddha-fields are known to be but a single buddha-field;
though they do not enter into one another, this is the Buddha’s supernormal power.
Knowing that all phenomena are unborn, one is able to give rise to the bodhicitta;
because all sentient beings are born in this way, it is called the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
To speak of patience as supernormal power means that even the essence of the dharma of patience is exhausted.
Entering into all phenomena, they likewise have no place of abiding.
Abiding in the spiritual powers of the Buddha, they have no doubt regarding any phenomenon;
having no doubt, they realize the non-arising of phenomena, and thus they receive their prophecy.
In order to bring sentient beings to maturity, one should purify the Buddha-fields;
through practice over many eons, one shall attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
Realizing that all Buddhas are empty, one knows that this is the supreme of all things.
Having crossed to the other shore of the Buddha-dharma for the sake of maturing sentient beings,
one is able to realize both the words and the meaning of the Buddha’s voice and supernormal powers;
within the secret teachings, one thus attains the crossing to the other shore.
Boundless and ungraspable, there is likewise no one who fully knows it;
such are the Buddha’s supernormal powers, which have no further limit.
If one realizes this for oneself, that itself is the supreme gift.
The supreme among all forms of giving is that which does not lead to rebirth in evil realms.
One who is able to practice every kind of giving, when constantly bestowing gifts,
possesses no discriminatory cognition and has no place of abiding.
Having understood this teaching, there is nothing that he does not relinquish;
throughout all births, for this reason, he abandons everything.
If, having heard this Dharma, one is able to relinquish the notion of a self,
Having taken [it], one is without attachment; this is the supreme generosity (*dāna*).
Having heard [the Dharma], one is free from feverish affliction; body and mind attain tranquility—this is the supreme ethical discipline (*śīla*), beyond which there is nothing superior.
Within the single dharma of emptiness, there is neither endurance nor contention;
this is the supreme patience, unsurpassed therein.
Having realized that all phenomena are empty, one possesses no heart of cowardice.
This is supreme diligence, wherein none can surpass it.
Always undisturbed within emptiness, awakening the mind in all things—
this is the blissful meditative concentration, manifested solely through sound.
If one is not afraid of emptiness, if one possesses omniscience and is free from conceptualization,
and if one is devoid of sloth and ignorance, such wisdom is supreme.
Through these various practices of the perfections, one enters into this teaching.
If one knows there is no verbal expression, one has already crossed all crossings.
Without destroying any phenomena, and without any affliction, one knows the True Dharma: the samādhi of effortless wisdom.
Not destroying any phenomena, nor being oppressed by them,
because of the tranquility of non-knowing, one crosses to the further shore of giving.
If one does not destroy phenomena, nor oppress phenomena, [one attains liberation].
This is the most supreme precept, the highest among all precepts.
If one does not destroy material things, and likewise regarding what is not the Dharma,
having become free from doubt in this way, one will no longer fall into the evil realms.
If one endures because it is inexhaustible, awakening to all conditioned phenomena,
this is the most supreme endurance, which cuts off all strife.
Constantly practice and draw near to this endurance, without ceasing day or night.
Thus, through bodily contact and realization, one shall obtain a pleasing form.
When practicing emptiness, if one does not give rise to thoughts of weariness,
this is supreme diligence, which abandons all sloth.
If one can physically touch such diligence as this,
it is called supreme diligence, unsurpassed by anything else.
It is not attached to empty phenomena, nor to meditative absorption or cessation.
This is the most supreme emptiness, far removed from all conceptualization and discursive thought.
Those who find joy in this dhyāna abandon all afflictions;
having thus touched it with the body, they are immediately free from restlessness.
If, regarding internal and external phenomena, there is no dependence or attachment, this is the most supreme wisdom, which no wisdom can disperse.
One should contemplate all phenomena: where there is no place for wisdom, [that is the ultimate state].
Having thus perceived through contact, one is not stained by or attached to any worldly things.
Knowing thus according to reality, one is always able to give everything, yet there is no "everything" given; therein, nothing is grasped.
All phenomena are non-existent; this is the very essence of all phenomena.
Having realized that there is nothing to be contacted, one is called a possessor of wealth.
If one’s reflection is cool and one skillfully cultivates equanimity, [one attains liberation].
Free from all timidity, cutting through doubt and shining everywhere,
dwelling purely within the precepts, they are free from the torment of feverish distress;
if there is nothing to be realized, their precepts remain unchanging.
Liberation is like space; there is nothing further to be seen.
As pure as space, it is therefore free from remorse.
Seeing no phenomena whatsoever, one seeks the unsurpassed path.
For the sake of all sentient beings, wherever afflictions arise,
one does not perceive those various bodies; when those bodies are not perceived,
there is no locus for the bondage of afflictions, and liberation is entirely like a dream.
Nothing further is seen, and that which is non-existent is likewise not seen;
therefore, it is called "like a dream.
Such distinctions as existence and non-existence are conceptual constructions arising from the auditory consciousness and its discursive investigation.
Just as space cannot be grasped,
so too the happy and miserable realms are but deluded and false conceptualizations;
in these places, there is no reality.
Through conceptualization one perceives that [object], yet therein nothing exists;
such is the true nature of form.
A person cannot be found, for internally there is nothing at all.
The external, too, cannot be apprehended.
Therefore it is said to be empty; one who can understand emptiness shall realize nirvāṇa.
That form has no substantial reality; if it is conditioned by that which does not exist, then for that non-existent thing there is no cause.
Its intrinsic nature is empty and quiescent; there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
There is no discarding, nor is there resemblance;
all faculties are capable of endurance. If one attains such patience as this, they shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
I beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, who later bestowed upon me this prediction:
"You shall go forth and attain Buddhahood.
As well as those good women—such as these did they awaken.
Then it shall not be difficult;
desiring to transform this female body, one should understand the body in this way,
and immediately one's vows will be fully realized.
Of handsome appearance and exceedingly upright, those who see him feel joy; such is the person, the *pudgala*.
One who understands this teaching, who practices with right conduct and right mindfulness, and who, having heard and retained it, is able to reflect upon it, is called a wise person.
For the sake of the multitude, he resolves the net of doubts;
for those whose minds are unsettled by uncertainty and who seek wisdom,
he is able to sever their doubts.
Causing them to abide upon the true path, you are able to provide illumination for all sentient beings dwelling in the darkness.
Attaining clarity in every place, you are beloved by all living beings.
By awakening to this teaching,
one’s faculties will be fully complete; one will always be born into a noble lineage,
and one’s retinue will all be harmonious and compliant.
For the sake of all benefit, and for the sake of other sentient beings as well, cause them all to abide in bodhi.
One should be able to swiftly realize and perceive this oneself; all sentient beings ought to [do so].
Always reverently serving others,
they are worthy of receiving all offerings; always being virtuous men,
they serve as shrines for the world.
Toward all supreme gifts, toward the unsurpassed World-Honored One,
they are worthy recipients; having subdued all worlds,
they shall become fields of merit.
One who can diligently practice will swiftly realize all the teachings of the Buddhas;
this is what is taught in this sūtra.
Suchness is free from conceptual discrimination; for the sake of this benefit, the Dharma is taught.
When practicing the conduct of enlightenment for incalculable eons,
it is because of hearing this teaching;
desiring to receive all the fruits of retribution, one is thus able to hear this Dharma.
One should diligently practice to realize it swiftly;
by taming all sentient beings, one will always possess majestic authority among all other multitudes.
Having well obtained this lifespan, and having encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, they are able to hear this teaching.
They understand the inconceivable; they act as śrāvakas for its sake.
Furthermore, one attains the merit of the Saṃgha.
Again, having relinquished one's own internal self, one should listen to the Sūtras;
having heard them, one should realize and understand them.
In this state there is nothing to be said; such are all these dharmas as they are explained herein.
There is neither gain nor loss, and no place from which anything can be brought forth.
This Dharma has no place of abiding; all Buddhas of the past have taught it thus, and any Buddhas of the future shall teach it in this same way.
The present Honored One among Two-legged Beings, and the Dharma teachings he proclaims,
are likewise non-dual.
Those who are able to expound this Dharma should do so just as I have taught.
One should thus awaken to this;
thereby one shall attain nirvāṇa, never failing to realize it,
and shall abide in bodhi.
This is the vision of all Buddhas; such is the nature of all dharmas and such is the locus of this vision.
When seeking within the realm of sentient beings, it is difficult to encounter its manifestation.
The true essence is empty and tranquil; all phenomena lack substantiality, and even phenomena themselves do not exist.
All that exists is quiescent; one knows this and that as they truly are.
All phenomena have no place of attainment; there is nothing that can be asked, and nothing that can be spoken.
This is called "non-existence," for one thus recollects the Tathāgata.
Again he asked the Supreme among Men:
"How can one perceive that which is invisible and speak of it?
Who is able to awaken to that which cannot be known?"
Together with the fourfold assembly, they joined their palms with ten fingers together and listened with tranquil minds.
They were without anything to be attained, being free from both ignorance and any locus of attainment.
When many people dwell with this intention,
they give rise to the desire for it, exert diligent effort,
and shall thereby come to know what has been heard.
True wisdom is non-conceptual; as it is with oneself, so it is with all—thus does the Truth speak.
Beholding these great supernormal powers, all give rise to a mind of joy.
They shall attain supreme enlightenment;
having awakened and realized it for themselves, they will be as I have described— numbering in the hundreds of nayutas.
All those who have heard the Dharma, numbering twice a hundred thousand,
have already touched and realized the true Dharma; they have all attained harmony together,
having previously heard and awakened to this Dharma under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having heard this and now having realized it through direct contact, they shall all become Buddhas;
just as I am now situated here, they shall preach the Dharma in this very way,
without any increase or decrease.
In former places of birth, he once heard such a Dharma as this,
never before encountered.
Through the explanation of non-existence, he has already entered the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
Now, understanding the meaning of what has been heard,
he feels revulsion toward his own body; seeing himself as belonging to the lowest class,
and knowing the Buddha’s supernormal powers, he again gains faith and enters deeply.
The inconceivable and so forth—having entered therein, one immediately attains them.
Neither dharma nor non-dharma; this is the Buddha’s supernormal power, supreme among all worlds. Having awakened to non-conceptuality, [one realizes it].
There is nothing that cannot be attained.
Having heard what was heard, those of sharp faculties have explained to me the essential nature of the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Enshrouded by the net of delusion, though they have heard [the teachings] for a long time,
they do not know the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
Realizing that he is the supreme among men, they awaken to this great supernormal power.
Thereafter, I received the prediction:
"During an incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), I encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
because I understood conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being characterized by something to be attained."
Overwhelmed by what they have attained, they cling to the notion of a self;
deluded by various afflictions, they do not perceive the Buddha’s supernormal powers.
Because they harbor attachments, they wander through the cycle of birth and death.
Their number cannot be reached by any limit;
such is the supernatural power of the Buddhas, and those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have been attached to it for a long time as well.
If you wish to swiftly realize bodhi, the tranquil supernatural powers of a Buddha,
you should quickly aspire to enter awakening.
Though one may be called a "harm-doer," one will instead gain the faculty of beneficial wisdom.
"Therefore, it is not difficult for them to attain it.

At that time, the Devaputra Avṛha from within the assembly immediately scattered various celestial *mandārava* flowers over the Buddha, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
For what reason?
This person of evil mind, difficult to tame and a murderer of people, possesses such sharp faculties and subtle wisdom that he is able to reach such swift and decisive understanding.
Having spoken these words,
the Buddha then addressed the Devaputra Avṛha, saying:
"Devaputra, listen attentively!"
This evil-minded one, difficult to tame and a slayer of people, in past lives for five hundred births, received the body of a venomous serpent; upon seeing [beings], he would harm them.

Having received that body, throughout day and night, many sentient beings were harmed by him; because of the torment of hunger, they all devoured him until he was exhausted, yet even then he could not be satisfied. Once consumed, he perished, becoming nothing but ashes.
Because he cannot find food, he fails to sleep; his body lacks peace and comfort, and his evil mind increases further.
Whether it be for a day and night, a fortnight, a month, or even years, due to that evil mind he meets his end and immediately falls into the Avīci Hell.

Having been born there, they undergo great suffering for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of years; when they cast off that body, they are reborn among the snakes that kill upon sight, and thus passing through five hundred successive lifetimes, they shall constantly assume the bodies of snakes that kill upon sight.

"If he abandons that body and is reborn again in the Avīci Hell, it is because such an accumulation of evil has arisen; furthermore, in his final birth, being bound by the maternal affection for that mother of poisonous snakes, he kills various insects and gives them to her to eat. Once she has eaten her fill and her body has attained comfort, she then falls asleep, remaining unaware of day or night."

While he was asleep, his mother killed many insects—perhaps as many as a thousand—and having taken their lives, she placed them all around him on every side and also by his mouth, forming a great heap.

Once he has awakened from sleep, he eats those various worms until his body is moistened and fully satiated; having regained a sense of well-being, he immediately falls back asleep for seven days and nights.
During those seven days and nights, his mother again kills hundreds of thousands of worms and places them by his mouth, forming a great heap.
After he had woken from his sleep, while he was still eating that heap of insects and had not yet finished, he saw his mother killing more insects and bringing them back to form another heap.
He then had this thought:
"How extraordinary!

My mother has performed a difficult task; out of love for me, she sought out so many insects to give me as food. Yet I do not know satisfaction now, nor do I know their limit as I eat them all. I ought not to seek food in such a way that causes my mother, out of love for me, to seek it for my sake."
"What can I now do to repay my mother?

Thinking thus, he gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward his mother; recognizing her benefit and her kindness, he immediately gave rise to a heart of affection and a heart of wishing to provide for her welfare.
That nourishment moistened his body;
furthermore, because he had conceived a heart of loving-kindness toward his mother, he became somewhat supple and moist, and as he fell asleep, his body and mind were at peace and happy.
At that time, some wood-gatherers encountered him and all saw him together; they immediately severed his life-faculty with sharp axes.
"After he has passed away, there will be a candāla named Āśvāsa who will be born into that son's family, yet he will still harbor an evil mind.
At that time, after the grandfather Āśvāsa has died, the son of Āśvāsa will in turn be executed."

Later, at another time, that son’s life ended after he had exhaled that breath; once his life had ended, this karma was exhausted, for there is no one who executes those whose death is ordained by destiny.
At that time, the minister addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty should know that the chief executioner named Qi xu has passed away, and his son has also passed away."
"Great King, you should know that there is currently no one who kills one who deserves death.
At that time, the king said to his ministers:
"Is there any clan among the Vāṣpamukhas who has already received their hereditary inheritance and means of livelihood?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"At that gate where the breath is exhaled, there is currently an orphaned son who has inherited his family’s estate.
The king commanded the minister, saying:
"You all may go and bring that orphaned son here to see me.
Having received the command, the ministers brought him before the king.
The king commanded him, saying:
“O youth! Since you have now received the breath of life and the worldly means of livelihood, why do you not practice the execution of those who deserve death?
He replied to the king:
"I respectfully follow Your Majesty’s command; however, I have relatives who will not permit me to kill them.
If Your Majesty now sends me back from this retreat, I shall return home for a moment and come back again immediately."
The King said: "Young man!
You may know the proper time; you should come quickly."
Having arrived home, he took the lives of all his wives, children, and kinsmen; then, returning to the king's presence, he addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should know that I have slaughtered all my relatives; there is no one left who can obstruct me from killing."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will command me as to what I should do.
Thereupon, the king immediately handed over swords, staves, and instruments of execution, yet he still would not accept them.
The king commanded him once more, saying:
"Why do you now refuse to accept the sword and staff?
He replied to the king, saying: "Great King!"
Since I am now known as one who knows how to execute those deserving of death, I possess my own fangs and have no need for swords or staves.

Great King, you should know that if one lacks the strength of teeth, they must rely on weapons; but I have fangs, and for those who deserve to die, I shall bite them with my teeth to sever their lives. Having drunk their blood, it shall nourish and moisten my body, increasing my vital energy.

Thereupon, he immediately seized a person condemned to death, bit their neck with his teeth to sever their life, and drank their blood. Having drunk the blood, his physical strength doubled, and his fierce majesty and malevolence increased even further.

“Good son! That person who was difficult to subdue and a killer of others, at that time, had killed many sentient beings and drunk their blood; his evil mind was fiercely blazing and his mental faculty was sharp and keen. Possessing such sharp intelligence, he heard the name of the Bodhisattva ‘Non-existence,’ and questioned the World-Honored One regarding the meaning of emptiness to sever the outflows (*āsrava*). He did not give rise to afflictions, inversions, or discursive discrimination; he severed the intent of anger, stinginess, greed, and envy, and was able to completely destroy all places devoid of kindness and righteousness, thereby attaining the state beyond words.”

When hearing the explanations from the Buddha, having heard them, one further increases one's sharp wisdom and enters into the great supernormal powers of all Buddhas; thus, one attains such superior benefits and merits.

At that time, there was another bodhisattva mahāsattva named Upadeśaka who rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha, desiring to ask a question.

As he joined his palms, through the Buddha’s supernormal power, various exquisite flowers growing on land and in water that were in bloom—possessing subtle colors and fragrances—filled his hands. He immediately felt immeasurable joy and exultation; with a joyful mind, he scattered those flowers over the Buddha. Having scattered them three times, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Has this man, who is so difficult to tame and who kills others, already given rise to the bodhicitta?
Then the Buddha said to him:
"O son of good family!"
"You should instead question this one who is difficult to subdue and who kills and harms others; that son of good family will explain it for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāsanavidhi again joined his palms and asked him, saying:
"O son of good family!
"Have you already generated the bodhicitta? He replied:
"O son of good family!"

I know that my present resolve for bodhicitta is pure and free from turbidity; just as I immediately severed all evils upon hearing of the Buddha’s great supernormal powers, so too have I now heard this inquiry by the Bodhisattva No-Ownership and the World-Honored One’s explanation thereof. Having heard it, I accept it with faith, maintain it in mind, and contemplate it without the net of doubt.

Regarding that which the Blessed One has taught: all phenomena are empty and without self, without arising and without ceasing, and without any objective sphere; where there is no objective sphere, there is no place of space.
"O son of good family!
What kind of mind do you intend to arouse in this place as you listen?
The Teacher Bodhisattva asked him again:
“O son of good family!
To what extent have you brought sentient beings to maturity for enlightenment? He then replied:

“Good son! Regarding those immeasurable, inconceivable, and otherwise unassailable sentient beings, I have brought them to maturity and established them in the seeds of enlightenment; throughout boundless eons, I shall continue to further mature all sentient beings.”
"Good son! Just as space has great capacity for containment, so too does the Buddha-dharma contain the immeasurable.
If one has faith and acceptance, they can bring others to maturity; they can also mature all sentient beings, ensuring they do not cling to deviant paths or commit evil deeds."
“Good son! I have taken as my object of focus the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings; what I now tell you is without falsehood, as the Buddha himself has personally realized and known.”
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not bestow a prediction upon me, I shall personally predict my own attainment of bodhi. Why is this?

I have already entered with faith into the seed of a bodhisattva; I abide in the patience of faith, free from doubt and confusion. Within these great supernormal powers of all Buddhas, this is that which all bodhisattvas share equally without attachment: the arousal of the mind of bodhi as the very foundation.

Once it has increased, one will be able to realize the fruit of enlightenment and omniscience in succession; one shall awaken to and know all Buddha-dharmas, gradually bring immeasurable sentient beings to maturity, and likewise achieve accomplishment on the path to enlightenment, abiding within the Bodhisattva’s immovable dharma.
“Good son! It is so, it is so!
There is no difference and no distinction.

One who is able to act thus may bring forth all manner of marks; yet, so that sentient beings may conceive a sense of weary detachment and be free from doubt, they shall enter the sphere of the Buddha’s great supernormal powers and personally behold a small portion of me.”
Why is this? Because that Buddha’s supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are immeasurable. Good son!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to discern and perceive through their great supernormal powers; as for the bodhisattvas, those who have not yet attained patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) proceed solely by means of faith, whereas those bodhisattvas who have attained patient acceptance have already entered into a small portion of the Buddha’s supernormal powers.

At that time, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, this great earth shook in six ways, becoming peaceful, blissful, and moist; not a single sentient being was struck with fear, and all musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
From above, the void rained down *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
In the sky, various celestial garments appeared spontaneously, hanging down and manifesting, while burning all manner of incense belonging to the devas and humans.

All those bodhisattvas from every one of those trichiliocosm world systems, being unable to discern their limits, gathered handfuls of these flowers and scattered them over the Buddha; they did so a second and a third time, and likewise scattered them over this assembly.

At that time, there further emerged from the earth sixteen koṭis of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of lotuses, each as large as a chariot wheel; upon the calyxes of those flowers sat bodhisattvas, all fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

Those bodhisattvas each descended from their flowers and, in turn, scattered these flowers over the Buddha. Having made this floral offering, they stood before the Buddha with palms joined in reverent salutation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śāsanavidhi, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed those bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
From where have you come?"
That bodhisattva said:
"I have come here from worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as incalculable asaṃkhyeyas, having attended upon and paid homage to incalculable Buddhas and heard their Dharma."
The Teacher of Bodhisattvas asked them again: "Virtuous sons!
What Dharma have you heard?"
They replied to him, saying:

"We too have heard that there is a bodhisattva named No-Thingness-Questioning, for whom the Buddha provides an explanation; it is just like the teachings explained by Śākyamuni Tathāgata here, and likewise without any increase or decrease."
That bodhisattva is also named "Nothingness," and he questioned that Buddha.

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, likewise spoke thus: "Do not give rise to afflictions; cause the severing of doubts and delusions; cause the production of light; and cause one to draw near to all Buddhas and the peerless Dharma of omniscience."
At that time, the great assembly gave rise to a sense of rare wonder and all thought to themselves:

"Those people have truly attained a human body and truly attained a long life; they have encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world and followed the Buddhas. Having heard such teachings as these asked by the Bodhisattva No-Thingness, they have entered them with faith and practiced accordingly, remaining without signs, without attainment, and without giving rise to afflictions."
World-Honored One!
We have now well attained great benefit; we have well attained a human body and well attained a long life.

Now that we have heard the questions posed by the Bodhisattva No-Thingness and the Buddha’s explanation thereof, our ears have heard it and we have understood it with faith; we are free from doubt and have attained direct realization.
Now that I have attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), I too shall likewise bring benefit to all sentient beings and provide them with a wholesome, universal shelter.

Even if we were now to fill this trichiliocosm with every kind of precious jewel and offer it as a gift, we still could not repay the virtue of this Bodhisattva *Akiṃcanya*, who, without manifesting his physical form, was able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the dharma of tranquility and was able to sever the doubts and perverted views of immeasurable sentient beings.
"What should we now do to make offerings to this one who does not manifest his body?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Niṣkiṃcana spoke these words:
"O sons of good family!
If you, upon hearing such teachings as these, are able to believe and understand them, you will have already performed the most sublime and wondrous offering to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

I have now asked this question, and the Buddha has provided its explanation. If you all attain a state free from doubt and free from feverish affliction, then at the time you realize Bodhi, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, for the sake of liberating those who are attached, and also for the sake of transforming those malicious enemies who seek to harm others—[you shall do so].
It is for these few reasons that I have questioned and entreated the Tathāgata; I have now revealed the teachings of all the Buddhas and have illuminated all the darkness of ignorance.
At that time, those with evil minds who were difficult to tame, enemies, and murderers, having seen such great supernormal powers as these, thought:
"Just as he knows, he does not grasp at high or low; his mind is tamed and compliant, free from joy or anger."
When these words were spoken, the Unsubduable Foe immediately leaped into the air from that spot and said:
"O sons of good family!

All phenomena are like illusions and transformations; they possess no reality and are merely products of conceptual construction. The true essence of all phenomena is suchness (*tathatā*), immovable and free from inversion. Therefore, you should abandon all mental conceptions that you maintain and establish.

Such perceptions as these lack any real perception; they are inverted perceptions and not perceptions based on reality. Therefore, you have now reached the state free from doubt, and you shall also attain unimpeded eloquence.
"Since you have already been liberated from all doubts, when seeking Bodhi, you shall not rely on others, but shall always achieve full awakening through your own self.
Then the World-Honored One said:
"O sons of good family!"
Excellent! Excellent!
It is just as you have said.
At that time, the ill-behaved and malevolent enemy addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I am now granted a prediction of enlightenment, for I have received the World-Honored One’s praise of 'Excellent'."

Although the Blessed One has granted this prediction to me alone, it causes this great assembly to leap for joy; their minds are filled with gladness so that they may further develop a superior resolve and become free from timidity.
"Blessed One!
I do not now see that dharma with which I might rejoice and leap for joy.
Blessed One!"

All phenomena are devoid of thought and lack any true reality; they arise from conceptual discrimination, and it is through this discrimination that they appear adorned, like magical illusions, like what is seen in a dream, or like a whirling firebrand.

I have realized these things as they truly are, following the explanation given by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to the Bodhisattva *Nāsti-kimcana*, because I am neither compliant nor non-compliant.
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Nothingness, Scroll Two.
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Nothingness, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta and others during the Sui Dynasty.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and golden light issued from his mouth, ascending as far as the Brahma-world to illuminate the entire trichiliocosm;
it circled the Buddha three times and returned to enter through the crown of his head.

At that time, there was a bodhisattva among the assembly named Anupalipta (Unstained). He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do you now manifest a smile?
Since no Tathāgata, Buddha, or Arhat ever smiles without a cause or condition, we pray that you will explain it so as to bring joy to the assembly.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Arakta: "Good son!

This difficult-to-tame enemy who has killed and harmed others shall, after the passing of eighty-nine hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in a future age, attain Buddhahood. He shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śikharaguṇa; he shall appear in the world as the One Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

"Good son! As for this enemy with an unruly and evil mind who previously harmed you, after his life has ended here, he shall be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven in the presence of Bodhisattva Maitreya, remaining there for as long as that bodhisattva’s lifespan lasts."

When Maitreya Bodhisattva was born into this world, he at that time became a great elder with immeasurable wealth and merit; all his karmic fruits and rewards were fully manifested, and for twenty days and nights, he made offerings to the World-Honored One Maitreya and his assembly of śrāvakas.

Having beheld the splendors of the adornments of the Buddha-field of the World-Honored One Maitreya, he immediately gave rise to a yearning aspiration. Desiring to accomplish such adornments of a Buddha-field, together with his retinue, he invited the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Maitreya, who was surrounded by a host of śrāvakas before and behind him. For three months, he presented all manner of offerings and instruments of pleasure, serving, honoring, respecting, and making offerings to them with the utmost reverence. He then took a plain cloth eighty cubits in length and painted upon it the image of the Tathāgata Maitreya, as well as the features of the adornments of that Buddha-field.
Having completed the paintings, he made an offering to the World-Honored One, Maitreya Tathāgata, and immediately made this vow:

"By means of this merit, may I attain such adornments of a Buddha-field as these; may my Buddha-field possess all the marks of complete adornment, just as those possessed by the present World-Honored One Maitreya, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. May the śrāvakas in my Buddha-field be fully endowed with wisdom, and may the bodhisattvas in my Buddha-field be fully endowed with immeasurable wisdom."
Having made this vow, they scattered flowers of gold and silver over the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Maitreya, and further spoke these words:

"We shall likewise practice such diligence and shall likewise achieve the adornment of such Buddha-fields as those of the former World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the Victorious King of the Śākya clan, who manifested radiant illumination for our sake; and at that time, he brought immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings to maturity in Bodhi, just as the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One Maitreya, has many hosts of bodhisattvas."
"In that first assembly of the Tathāgata Śreṣṭhārtha, the bodhisattvas were immeasurable, and through their bestowal of predictions, they all attained patience.
In the second assembly, the multitude of bodhisattvas was again twice as immeasurable."
In the third assembly, there will again be twice as many as the immeasurable [number mentioned before]; such are the skillful means.

That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Guṇottama will have such a multitude of bodhisattvas, and that Tathāgata Guṇottama will instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden those bodhisattvas, causing them to practice their vows.
"Once they have attained the initial resolve, I shall cause them all to achieve omniscience and even reach enlightenment. 'Good son!

As for these difficult-to-tame enemies who previously harmed others, after they encounter the appearance of Maitreya Buddha in the world, their lifespans in all places of birth shall be immeasurable—except during the period when they are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), when their lifespan is twenty years; yet even in that state, within a single day, they will personally undergo the immeasurable suffering and affliction resulting from all their evil karma.'"
From this point forward until the attainment of enlightenment, they shall further cultivate the awakening to bodhi, and once having awakened to bodhi, their lifespan shall be immeasurable.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for an immeasurable time, and there shall be no age of evil.

As for me today, among these deceitful and evil sentient beings—those who speak wickedly, those lacking wisdom, those difficult to lead into the Path, and those possessed by Māra—I now preach the Dharma and teach them; yet such beings find it difficult to understand and difficult to enter.
This good man, however, is free from all such afflictions and difficulties.
"Good son! In that buddha-field, there are no māras or demonic activities.
All sentient beings of sharp faculties and great agility have gathered there; therefore, when the Tathāgata of superior merit preaches the Dharma, they attain understanding with little effort."

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Unobstructed Pure Moon (*Anāvaraṇaviśuddhacandra*). He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and joined his palms toward the Buddha. Desiring to resolve his own doubts and to cause this assembly to sever theirs as well, he addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“I ask the Lamp of the World, The one of unimpeded mass of wisdom, Desiring to sever my own doubts And for the sake of this assembly.”
For what reason does this assembly see that even those of sharp faculties,
who previously killed and harmed others, have now received the prediction of enlightenment?
Great Naga, please explain their past deeds and karma.
Having already spent billions of kalpas constantly dwelling in the realms of evil destinies,
and having accumulated [suffering] over many kalpas because they were shrouded by the blindness of ignorance,
they have constantly endured manifold sufferings for many hundreds of billions of kalpas.
Wandering through the cycle of birth and death, where the fires of hell blaze fiercely,
they cry out "Abhica! Beholding their karma to be thus,
they undergo twice as much suffering within birth and death, receiving the bodies of evil venomous snakes.
Upon seeing [them], one is able to kill them, [committing] many hundreds of billions of births and deaths.
Having undergone manifold sufferings for many hundreds of billions of kalpas,
even if one is born among human beings, one again becomes a person who kills others.
Now that I have been able to see the World-Honored One, my faculties have immediately become sharp;
I have swiftly severed all afflictions and resolved my mind upon Bodhi.
Having received the Buddha’s prophecy, for as many as incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), I shall [abide].
He shall become a lamp for the world; fame and renown are the supreme merit.
He explained those past events to the best of men:
such were his deeds, and such was the bitter fruit of his evil karma.
Throughout these hundreds of millions of eons, you have already endured manifold sufferings;
whatever wholesome karma you possess, your Teacher has also explained it to you,
as well as all the practices you performed in the past— both evil deeds and unwholesome ones.
The Lamp of the World perceives and illuminates all; I pray that you will speak for me.
O Great Man who cuts through doubt, for my sake and for the sake of sentient beings, as well as those of the future who are able to hear this teaching— [please explain].
If there are those who harbor doubts, or have uncertainty regarding this Dharma,
the Teacher shall now sever them.
For the sake of gathering in sentient beings, he addresses these sons of good family:
"Please speak of such past deeds, O you of great renown.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Pure Moon, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, noble son! It is well that you now wish to sever the doubts of the entire assembly by questioning the Tathāgata on such a matter as this.
"You, son of good family!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for you.
O son of good family!

Just as those various karmas performed in the past have caused such great numbers of sufferings to be endured throughout hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas, you, having heard this, should believe in the Tathāgata and not give rise to fear; you should uphold it single-mindedly and teach it exactly as instructed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Unobstructed Pure Moon addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! I recall that in the past, ninety billion nayutas of kalpas after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Dharmamati-rāja-saṃtuṣṭa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, up to Buddha, World-Honored One.”

The lifespan of that Buddha was sixty-eight thousand years; at his first assembly, there were sixty-two koṭis of hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas, and the number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas was twice as great.
That Buddha-world is named Brahmāpati, and the eon is named Pure Intention (*Vimalamati*). It was during that eon that the Tathāgata Dharmamati-prītirāja was born.
"For what reason is that eon called Pure Intention?"
In that eon, Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas constantly appear in the world; therefore, that eon is named "Pure Intention" (*viśuddhamati*).
Son of good family!

During the eon when that Tathāgata Dharmamati-nandirāja dwelt in the world, this son of good family, Difficult-to-Tame Enemy (*durdamāri*), was at that time a king named Subduer of Enemies (*ariṃdama*). He invited that Tathāgata, along with the community of bhikṣus and the assembly of bodhisattvas, and for three months he made offerings to that Tathāgata with every kind of requisite for pleasure. Having heard the Dharma from him, he resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Having planted roots of goodness, he further encountered ten thousand buddhas; in all places he constantly practiced the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), constantly attained great learning, and through diligent application of effort, achieved the four dhyāna concentrations.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, he again encountered a Tathāgata named Vajrajvālāprabha. In the presence of that Buddha, he left the household life to practice the Way, cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya), exerting diligent effort, and practicing the dhūta ascetic virtues, always dwelling in forest hermitages and secluded places.
"If one recites ten thousand sections of the sūtras, all of which are Mahāyāna, one will also attain the four dhyānas, the five supernormal powers, and the four formless absorptions. Good son!"
That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vajrajvāla has a community of ten koṭis of bhikṣus, all of whom are arhats.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of eighty-four *koṭi-nayuta-śata-sahasra* bodhisattvas who constantly followed the World-Honored One; they had all attained equal patience (*samaropa-kṣānti*) and *dhāraṇī*, turned the non-retrogressive wheel, and were well-versed in profound dharmas. They had already entered the boundless gates of *dhāraṇī* and were able to skillfully enter the ocean-seal samādhi (*samudra-mudrā-samādhi*) of the boundless dharma-realm. Sporting with supernatural powers, their minds had attained certainty; they manifested bodies sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas and constantly practiced compassion toward all sentient beings.

“Good son! At that time, among the assembly of the Buddha’s bodhisattvas, there was a leading bodhisattva bhikṣu and Dharma-master named Uttara-artha (Supreme Benefit). He was skilled in expounding the meaning of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening others, enabling all bodhisattvas to attain inconceivable and complete merit. He served as the attendant to that World-Honored One, constantly following him wherever he went or stayed, just like the bhikṣu Ānanda today, who is able to receive and uphold all the sūtras.”

“Good son! In this way, that Bodhisattva Superior Benefit was able to receive and uphold all the nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata Sovereign King, and he was able to explain their meaning for those many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of bodhisattvas.”

"Good son! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sovereign King, for twenty thousand years taught and transformed all bodhisattvas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and all sentient beings by preaching the Dharma. After those twenty thousand years were complete, he then addressed the Bodhisattva Beneficial Superior (Lābhottara) amidst a great assembly of all bodhisattvas, the community of bhikṣus, devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, saying: 'Good son!'"

"You should receive and uphold this inconceivable dharma of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, cultivated through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. In the future final age, for the sake of increasing the roots of goodness in all devas and humans, you must protect and maintain this dharma, manifesting and illuminating the Tathāgata’s teachings of enlightenment so that they may endure for a long time; therefore, receive, uphold, explain, and expound it."
“Good son! This night, at the half-watch, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, shall enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Upakāraśreṣṭha, hearing of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, wept with tears falling like rain. He rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“May the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings remain for one eon, Benefiting the world’s devas and humans alike.
I now entreat the Eye of the World: May you preach the sublime Dharma to instruct and guide us.”
O Guide of profound wisdom and freedom from affliction, Abiding in supreme conduct and all virtues,
The All-Seeing One who tames gods and humans— O Honored One of great supernormal powers, may you long remain!
If they hear that the Guide has entered parinirvāṇa, the devas and humans will be distressed in heart;
out of compassion for them, O Guide, we pray that you remain in the world to show us your instruction.

I and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, Oppressed by manifold sufferings and filled with grief and distress, All do so because the Teacher has proclaimed his final nirvana; The Kinsman of the World now intends to enter parinirvāṇa.

O Tamer of men, who brings others to discipline, I pray that you, the Honored One with the Universal Eye, may long remain, For the benefit of the world’s devas and humans; Thus do I now entreat the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to benefit the devas and the people of the world, replied to the Bodhisattva Benefactor Supreme (Upakāra-uttama) in verse:
“I have already brought benefit to the world, Teaching such doctrines as these;
I have already fulfilled all bodhisattvas, Causing them to abide in the outflow-free state of all Buddhas.”
This very night, during the latter part of the watch, I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
I now entrust this teaching of the Dharma to you, so that it may endure for a long time after the World-Honored One has passed away.
When that assembly had heard these words, all those bodhisattvas joined their palms and gazed together upon that Tathāgata.
Weeping with compassion and shedding tears like rain, they spoke thus:
"We pray only that the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings will console us and these hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."
"After the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, who will become a Buddha?
O World-Honored One, you are supreme above all worlds!
Out of compassion, he spoke with gentle words, consoling the devas and humans of the world:
“Do not harbor fear when I have passed away; after me, another Buddha shall appear in the world.
There is a bodhisattva named Guṇakara who, through his practice, has attained untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
In a future age he shall become a Buddha, a Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings named Jñānārcis.”
I now exhort you, know this well: for the sake of upholding this Dharma, may you extensively reveal and clarify such teachings of the Dharma for the sake of the world, including gods and humans.
Having heard the World-Honored One speak thus, he immediately offered words of consolation and further declared:
"This great supernormal power is most difficult to achieve;
because it embraces the Dharma that has no embracer, and out of my reverence for the Teacher, I now embrace the True Dharma."
I shall widely proclaim this Dharma teaching; I shall relinquish my body and my life, for by not guarding my own body or life, I may protect the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"If one does not cherish one's own body, one will then be able to protect the Teacher’s Dharma.
"O son of good family!

At that time, after that Buddha had comforted and gladdened the entire great assembly, and had taught the Dharma, given instructions, and bestowed his majestic power, he entered parinirvāṇa during the final watch of the night."

"Good son! After that World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, that bodhisattva preached eighty thousand dharma-gates to bring them to fulfillment. In this way, he brought sentient beings to accomplishment; many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings were matured for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. How much more so those who abide in the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and how much more so those who plant roots of goodness while wandering in saṃsāra?"

“Good son! After that Buddha-Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa and the True Dharma has been extinguished, during the period of the Semblance Dharma there will be many bhikṣus who claim that [existence] can be attained and that [suffering] can be extinguished; they will take no pleasure in upholding these sūtras and will further give rise to slander against them.”
"Good son! At that time, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a king of men named Viryavikrama, whose karmic fruit was vast.
Then, that Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Anupamārtha went to the king’s abode and expounded the Buddha-dharma for him, teaching the secret teachings of the Tathāgata."

Having heard this, the king immediately conceived a heart of reverence and respect for the bhikṣu Upāriṣṭa, and he immediately resolved his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and made offerings to the bhikṣu.
And that bhikṣu, desiring to convert those sentient beings, accepts all offerings from every quarter without giving rise to weariness or regret, nor does he conceive a mind of fatigue.

"After that king had made offerings to that bhikṣu for a full three months, together with eighty-four thousand court ladies—each of whom was personally adorned and carried various incenses, flowers, musical instruments, precious necklaces, ointments, and garments—he thus offered such things to the bhikṣu and all his disciples, numbering eight thousand five hundred who always followed him in harmony; all of them attained non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

“Good son! At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Śāntavīrya-vinaya (Tranquil Dignity), who was a tamer of the unruly, an enemy, and a slayer of men. He was skilled in expounding the Dharma, possessed great learning and dhāraṇīs, and had mastered ten thousand sūtras and other texts. He recited and maintained them with fluency, was able to extensively analyze all the sūtras, and constantly taught the principles of few desires and contentment.”

That bhikṣu had already attained the four dhyānas, as well as the five supernormal powers and the four formless attainments; that bhikṣu of tranquil concentration and dignified deportment had a large following of five hundred who followed him, and they likewise possessed such dignified deportment and superior conduct.

"At that time, the bhikṣu Śānteryāpatha, seeing the bhikṣu Bodhisattva Upakāraśreṣṭha, was neither pleased nor delighted; he conceived an evil mind, gave rise to a state of anger, manifested a look of malice, and spoke these words before the assembly:
'Such a bhikṣu as this!'"
Where is there any practice of awakening?
Where is there any Dharma of the Buddhas?
Since such mixed practices lack even the proper deportment for conduct in the world, how much less could they possibly realize supreme wisdom?
Yet those people were single-mindedly devoted only to the bodhisattva bhikṣu Upakāra, and none could undermine them.
At that time, the bhikṣu Śānteryāpatha’s anger and resentment increased even further, and he turned his back on that place and departed, saying:
"I no longer wish to see such evil deeds; if this bhikṣu practices false views, he will cause all these people to fall into perversion."
When he reached the forest hermitage and intended to enter samādhi, because of his resentment, he was unable to enter any of those samādhis, let alone attain stability therein.

Due to such forceful exertion, all his meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), absorptions (*samāpatti*), and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) were entirely lost. Because of that mind of malice and hatred, he contracted a grave illness.
At that time, the bhikṣu Bodhisattva Hitopakarottama thought to himself: "How extraordinary!
Even such a bhikṣu as this has given rise to a great, unwholesome, and turbid mind of anger; I should now feel compassion for him and act for his benefit so that he may hear the profound Dharma."
At that time, the bodhisattva bhikṣu Anarthavighātin and his retinue of five thousand bodhisattvas soared into the air, remained there, and spoke these verses:
“The nature of the household life is said to be awakening; Desire is non-discriminative and indestructible.
If one awakens to this practice and expounds it, That awakening is the unsurpassed peace of awakening.”
The nature of the disposition of anger is like bodhi; this the World Teacher, the Wise One, has already explained.
If one awakens to such a practitioner of the Dharma, that awakening is bodhi, the supreme among bipeds.
Ignorance manifests as awakening and so forth; awakening and ignorance have no distinct nature.
This manifestation of ignorance through a single practice—this is how one should realize the unsurpassed path of awakening.
If there were those who have already explained the practice of views, as well as that supreme awakening of bodhi—
if one speaks of these two practices, then through the practice of views, one shall not attain bodhi.
The Dharma of all Buddhas is profoundly subtle; it cannot be known or seen through attainment.
Free from conceptual discrimination and any basis for reliance, those of skillful wisdom awaken to bodhi.
If one can relinquish all conceptual constructions, as well as pride regarding ethical discipline and views,
and abandon self-conceit based on extensive learning— having cast these aside, one awakens to bodhi.
It would be better to dwell at home, delighting in sensual desires, than to hear this Dharma and not be startled or doubtful,
but to have faith and understanding in the teachings spoken by the Guide and be able to expound them extensively through a single practice.

They do not leave the household life according to this teaching; dwelling in secluded places with views of attainment, they remain constantly bound by the notion of "I," giving rise to the thought: "I shall realize bodhi."
All conceptual thoughts that are expressed are but the snares of Māra;
if one knows all phenomena to be like space, then one will have no conceptual thoughts.
All Tathāgatas possess such a Dharma; all those with the Universal Eye speak of it as a single practice:
afflictions and awakening are non-dual, for neither affliction nor awakening can be apprehended.
If one does not discriminate between desire and hatred, nor discriminate between ignorance and the like,
having abandoned both and that which is other— those are the Teachers who awaken to Bodhi.
If one does not dwell upon anything attainable, nor possesses thought or agitation,
and does not give rise to the notion of self or rely on any basis, that awakening is the unsurpassed peace of bodhi.
If one abandons conceptualization within conceptualization, along with flattery, crookedness, illusion, deceit, and envy,
and delights in practicing the dhūta precepts and merit— such a person awakens to the immeasurable eye of Bodhi.
If one hears this Dharma without anything to discard, and does not doubt even when it is explained in detail,
that person shall swiftly become a Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, possessing unsurpassed wisdom and mastery in the world.
The most profound dharmas are supremely sublime, Inconceivable, tranquil, and free from outflows;
If one does not dispel the view of self, It will be difficult to awaken for many koṭis of eons.

“Good son! At that time, when the bhikṣu Bodhisattva Hitopakarottama spoke these verses, sixty-six nayutas of devas in the sky above attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).”
Furthermore, sixty-two thousand sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the bhikṣu Śānteryāpatha, having heard these verses, felt no sense of joy or pleasure; his mind became tormented with feverish distress, and his entire body swelled up.
Thereupon, that person instead gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness;

yet because they contemplate only this single instance of loving-kindness while regarding all others with hatred, at that moment the great earth splits open, and his current body falls into the Avīci Hell, where he remains for hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of years, undergoing extreme and great suffering.

Upon passing away from that life, they were immediately reborn among the venomous snakes; thus, through the course of many hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of births, they underwent the two evil states of existence: the Great Avīci Hell and the Raurava Hell.
He was reborn again among those poisonous snakes; because of such unwholesome roots, he remained there for a full sixty-two billion nayutas and hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

Because in the past he gave rise to a single thought of loving-kindness while gazing upon the Bodhisattva Uttara with his eyes, by virtue of those roots of goodness, he obtained a human body after passing away from that place; this was due to the habitual perfuming of that loving-kindness.

Furthermore, because he gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward that mother of poisonous snakes, and because he heard such profound and wondrous Dharma, he has now attained such sharp wisdom and supernormal powers.
“Good son, what do you think?
Was that bhikṣu of tranquil and dignified demeanor at that time anyone other than this person?”
This one who is now so difficult to subdue and full of enmity is that very person; he possessed such karmic obstacles in the past.
Noble son, what do you think?
At that time, the bodhisattva bhikṣu Hitopadeśa—do not entertain any other view—he was none other than myself.
O sons of good family!
At that time, the king named Vikramabala was none other than the present bodhisattva Akiṃcanya.
"O sons of good family!

It is because they gave rise to such feelings of anger and resentment toward Bodhisattvas in the past that they now undergo such difficult-to-comprehend, terrifying karmic obstructions and afflictions."
"O sons of good family!

For this reason, if there are bodhisattvas who wish to purify their various karmic obstructions, they should treat all other bodhisattvas with reverence and respect, regarding them as their teachers."
“Sons of good family!
If you wish to dwell in Bodhi without harming yourselves, you should train in this way.

When this Chapter on the Dharma Emerged in the Past was spoken, ninety-two nayutas of hundreds of thousands of sentient beings attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), and thirty-six billion nayutas of bodhisattvas purified their karmic obstacles.

At that time, the one who had previously harmed others—the Enemy Difficult to Subdue—heard the Buddha’s prophecy and leaped for joy. He flew up into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and spoke these verses:
“If one wishes to dwell in a pure land, One should act as the Teacher has instructed:
One should have faith in all Buddhas And their supreme, great supernormal powers.”
Having realized the Buddha’s supernormal powers, he knows that there is no state of non-discrimination;
such a thing does not exist in the world and is difficult to find.
If one hears that nothing exists, then regarding the sūtra and Dharma that have been asked about:
One who can believe, touch, and realize this, thereby makes offerings to all Buddhas.
Having studied this sutra, one can eliminate all notions of existence;
having attained equanimity and abandoned past evils, one shall behold the Guides.
If one studies this sutra, one thereby beholds all Buddhas and personally attends all Tathāgatas, as extensively explained in this sutra;
this is the perfection of giving, the foundation upon which pure ethical discipline rests.
Patience and diligence, wisdom and the other [perfections] are the fundamental bases.
If there is nothing to be grasped, this state cannot be described in words;
as the World-Honored One has taught, train yourself in such self-mastery.
If one hears this sutra, it causes all meanings to be revealed;
though one were to offer various kinds of worship until one’s strength is exhausted, there would be no way to repay it.
For incalculable many eons, one might remain in the dark, seeing nothing at all.
Those who hear this sutra shall attain the stage of all Buddhas.
They awaken from folly and shatter the darkness of ignorance;

"You have now told me that all things, all sentient beings, all bodhisattvas, and all buddhas are like shadows, illusions, dreams, mirages, echoes, and space; and that they are empty, signless, wishless, and effortless, detached from desire, quiescent, extinguished, and without reality."

All their karmic fruits and their names—all these are produced by us; they and I are all neither one nor two, neither many nor few, and are not substantial entities. They cannot be heard, are not possessed in common, and there is no one who can see them, no one who can know them, and no one who can hear them.

Therefore, you all! Listen to us, and with faith, understanding, reflection, and joy, acclaim it as excellent: those beings, numbering in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya, having practiced that which is unreal, are all unfindable; you also are unfindable. Do not slander us with falsehoods, and do not revile us.
Since we do not exist, and things have no characteristics and no location, for what purpose would it be necessary to speak for others? It would surely be better not to speak at all.

If there were someone who spoke, that [other] would still be just as it is, and this [self] would still be just as it is; thus, as one dispels it, so one dispels it, and having spoken thus, one returns just as one was.

At that time, having heard the meaning of these words, the great assembly became free from form and mind, free from inhalation and exhalation, and free from attachment to any thing; toward the Blessed One, they were entirely filled with every kind of joy.
Having attained their original mindfulness, they spoke these words:
"This is the reality of the essential nature; it is non-existent, there is nothing to be realized, and there is nothing to be cognized. Having known it thus, because there is no knowing."
So it is, so it is! From where could that have arisen?
It cannot be given a name.

At that time, in the space above, there was an immeasurable array of priceless jewels filling the interval. There were two bodhisattvas named Kṣayamkara and Anutpādadarśin who addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What auspicious sign is this, that these priceless jewels fill the entirety of space?
The Buddha said,
"O sons of noble family!

There are certain bodhisattvas who, having heard this dharma-gate of non-attainment and having thereby achieved liberation, have all already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena; it is for this reason that they manifest these signs.
At that time, the entire great assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
You are skillfully able to learn the wisdom of expedient means for the sake of liberating all sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
You are indeed able to know that all this is immovable, empty, and non-existent, and that there are no sentient beings, for their original nature is quiescent.
Yet now, the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings, explains that all dharmas are like shadows, while diligently laboring to teach and transform them.”
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is,
O sons of good family!
It is as you have said.
O sons of good family!

If there were no eloquent exposition, how could one know the dharmas of images, illusions, dreams, mirages, echoes, and space—those which are signless, wishless, effortless, and free from desire, such as nirvāṇa?
"And how do they become such phenomena as illusory images?
At that time, through the Buddha's majestic spiritual power, such a voice was heard from the sky above:
"World-Honored One!..."
"What is that reflected form which constitutes a reflection?
World-Honored One!
What is it, even down to its falsity, that constitutes a reflected form?"
World-Honored One!
This is already fully endowed with all adornments; the fundamental nature of dharmas does not require adornment.
World-Honored One!
For example, suppose a painter or a painter’s apprentice, having skillfully mastered his craft, were to paint an image of the Tathāgata, complete with all the marks and lacking nothing.

Then, a master goldsmith were to take the most excellent gold and fashion a golden crown for it to place upon its head; consequently, that image would become even more upright and beautiful, such that the entire multitude could gaze upon it without ever wearying.
"World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so. This very source of dharmas is complete with all marks; one may gaze upon it without ever being weary."
“The World-Honored One is now even more magnificently adorned.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha then addressed the voice from space, saying:

“It is like a skilled master of illusion or his disciple who is proficient in magical transformations; they conjure up men and women of upright and pleasing appearance, complete with all their faculties and in harmonious union, who then give birth to children and bestow names upon them.”
Like reflections, illusions, dreams, mirages, echoes, and the great void, they lack self-mastery.
Signlessness, wishlessness, non-action, detachment, tranquility, and nirvana—these are accomplished through the cultivation of such falsities.
Suppose there are many people who enter deep mountain valleys and each raises a loud voice, calling out to various reflections or even to empty space.

Once the sounds have been uttered, they vanish and do not appear; yet within that empty valley, there is nothing to which they are attached. At that time, though the multitude seeks the source of those sounds, it cannot be found at all.

In this way, all such afflictions and the like, when sought according to reality, cannot be found; they are like a shimmering mirage that appears to be water but cannot be drunk, and like an echo or a mirage that has no substantial form.
At that time, those among the assembly who had not yet realized the Dharma all attained realization upon hearing this teaching.
Twenty billion nayutas of devas and humans likewise all became unstained by and unattached to any phenomena.
At that time, a voice again issued from the void, and all the hosts of devas and humans saw and heard it:
"These are merely names, such as 'shadow' and so forth, even down to 'illusory images' and the like."
"Regarding whatever is asked concerning reflections and magical illusions, the Tathāgata has already realized and explained them.

When twenty billion devas and humans heard this Dharma, they all attained the certainty of abiding in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and shall act as friends for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Śrutidhara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what should this Dharma-text be named?”
"How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha said:
"This Dharma-text is named 'The Signlessness and Non-abandonment of All Transgressions'; receive and uphold it thus."
"Lordly Sovereignty of the Tathāgata"—thus it shall be upheld;
"The Inquiry of the Bodhisattva Nihilist"—thus it shall be upheld;
"The Exposition of the Great Supernatural Powers of the Buddha"—thus it shall be upheld.
"An evil mind is difficult to tame; one repents of enmity"—this is called upholding [the Dharma].
"There is no dharma that can be manifested"—this is called upholding [the Dharma].
"It is not that all dharmas are not seen"—this is called upholding [the Dharma].

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Bodhisattva Nothingness, as well as the Bodhisattvas Difficult-to-Tame-Enemy and Hearing-and-Holding, along with that great assembly—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—hearing what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, Scroll Four.
